dialogue_quality_notes: Participants propose concrete, practical rules (cleaning, extractor, booking) rather than abstract complaints.
Discussion proceeds in quick negotiated steps with clarifying questions ('Do you mean two fixed nights or two flexible slots?').
Minimal needless repetition; each turn added a small new element or acceptance.
evaluation.final_reason: Parties agreed on a combined compromise: a shared rule set posted on the whiteboard that allocates stove time and sets cleaning and ventilation expectations. Evidence: Agent D volunteered to write the rule and explicitly posted the agreed text: 'I'll put: "Two reservable weeknight slots per person (first-come); 24-hour swap; whoever cooks washes pans; use extractor and open window; quick heads-up if late or smelly."' Agent A accepted and performed the immediate cleaning ('Okay, I'll wash it now.'). Thus D wrote the concrete posting, A agreed to the cleaning obligation, and the group accepted whiteboard booking and heads-up rules in return for D's slot requests.
position_change_notes: Agent A moved from defensive stance ('close your door or tell me first') to accepting shared rules and the two-slot accommodation: 'I can agree to two weeknight slots...'.
Agent D moved from demanding slots ('I get two weeknight stove slots') to accepting the group's hygiene/ventilation rules and committing to post the agreed text on the whiteboard.

Agent B and Agent C largely held consistency: B pressed for ventilation and heads-up and accepted the whiteboard; C pressed for pan washing and asked for immediate compliance and for someone to post rules.

round_scores.evidence: Agent A proposes a rule but also tells others to 'close your door or tell me first instead of calling me out.' Agent B accepts the basic proposal but adds requirements: 'Also please turn on the extractor and open the window ... give a quick heads-up or avoid really smelly stuff.' Multiple substantive complaints (smell, cleaning) are active and not yet reconciled.

Agent C amplifies and formalizes B's suggestions and asks A to wash the pan now; Agent D introduces a new, substantive allocation demand: 'But can we also agree I get two weeknight stove slots each week so I’m not always left out?' This adds a scheduling/allocation conflict on top of cleaning and smell.

Agent A accepts 'two weeknight slots if we make a simple booking rule' and asks whether they should be fixed or flexible; Agent D defines 'Flexible slots' with reservable slots and a swap rule. The stove-allocation conflict remains but the parties are converging on a booking mechanism.

Agent A accepts 'two reservable weeknight slots with a 24-hour swap' and repeats the cleaning/ventilation/headsup requirements. Agent B prefers 'Whiteboard's easiest for me.' The main incompatibilities have mostly been narrowed to implementation details (whiteboard vs calendar).

Agent C asks who will write the rule and requests A wash the pan now. Agent D volunteers to write the rule and the two slots: 'I'll write the rule and the two weeknight slots on the whiteboard now.' These are small, operational outstanding items rather than substantive disagreement.

Agent A: 'Okay, I'll wash it now.' Agent D: explicitly states the text to be posted: 'I'll put: "Two reservable weeknight slots per person (first-come); 24-hour swap; whoever cooks washes pans; use extractor and open window; quick heads-up if late or smelly."' Everyone's prior demands are incorporated and no one objects, so the substantive conflicts are settled.

substantive_insights: The conflict combined normative (who should clean, courtesy norms about calling out) and practical (limited stove time) elements; resolving required addressing both.
Introducing a simple, implementable mechanism (whiteboard reservable slots + 24-hour swap) allowed competing access claims to be satisfied without complex arbitration.
Requiring cooks to wash their own pans and to use extractor/open window addresses the smell and cleaning complaints simultaneously, reducing incentives for repeated confrontation.
